title: How can hypermiling save you gas?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain why official EPA gas mileage ratings on new cars rarely match real-world driving. Cars are tested by automakers, with the EPA spot-checking 10 to 15 percent of new models, on dynamometers (treadmill-like rollers) using city and highway driving cycles, with an exhaust-carbon sensor used to measure fuel use. Lab conditions ignore wind resistance, weight, aerodynamics, aggressive acceleration, climate control, and poor maintenance, and the formula favors hybrids. They then cover hypermiling, a set of techniques popularized by Wayne Gerdes (spelled Gurtis in the transcript), including coasting, cruise control, slower highway speeds, turning off the engine when idling long, ridge riding, and distant anticipatory driving. They mention Edmunds tests and NASCAR fuel-saving tactics, and a caution about turning off keys on some cars. The episode closes with listener mail about the Peter Principle and demotion instead of firing, and a request to support military families.

segments.title: Opening banter and wedding talk
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about celebrity deaths, Chuck's Catholic wedding in Columbus, Ohio, and the episode topic of gas mileage.

segments.title: Why EPA mileage ratings are inflated
segments.summary: Automakers test their own cars and the EPA spot-checks about 10 to 15 percent of new models. Cars are tested on dynamometers with a professional driver following city and highway cycles, and fuel use is measured by a sensor in the tailpipe measuring carbon in the exhaust.

segments.title: Lab versus real-world driving
segments.summary: Lab tests ignore wind resistance, passengers, roof racks, weight, aerodynamics, aggressive acceleration, and maintenance. Cars are brand new and properly broken in, and the formula favors hybrids in city driving.

segments.title: Hypermiling techniques
segments.summary: Hypermiling, a term coined by Wayne Gerdes, is introduced. Edmunds found big gains, including cruise control and avoiding fast starts and hard braking. Other tips include coasting into parking spaces, turning off the engine when idling more than about seven seconds, ridge riding, and distant anticipatory driving. Speed, air conditioning, and open windows are also discussed.

segments.title: NASCAR fuel saving and cautions
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck note NASCAR drivers save fuel through cautions, coasting, and drafting. They caution listeners that on some cars turning the key off can lock the steering wheel, so keep the ignition in the accessory position.

segments.title: Listener mail: Peter principle and military families
segments.summary: Jennifer writes that her company demoted her from sales support to reception instead of firing her, and she keeps her pay. Another listener reports a similar case. She also asks the show to recognize military families.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck invite email feedback and point listeners to the HowStuffWorks site and blogs.
